---
title: "Pomodoro timer"
subtitle: "A 45-minute focus block, with the pets as the face of the timer"
---

DeskPets has a built-in focus timer. You start a 45-minute work block, and when it ends the pets celebrate and a chime plays. It is there because the pets are already on your screen, so the timer doesn't need another window, and the signal to take a break comes from something you're already looking at.

## Using it

Press the **play button** in the stats card header, or choose **Start Pomodoro** from the tray menu. While it runs, the card's subtitle counts down (`Focus · 44:59 left`) and the button turns into a stop square. Hover over the pets to see it.

## Cancelling gives up the block

There is **no pause**. If you start a work block and need to stop, pressing the stop square (or *Stop Pomodoro* in the tray) cancels it, and that block is gone. Starting again begins a fresh 45 minutes. This is deliberate: a block is only a block if you finish it.

## When it ends

- A chime plays.
- Layla and Chico play the *pleased* animation for **five minutes**.
- The card says `Pomodoro complete · take a break`.

The celebration outranks everything else the pets might be doing, including the grumpy animation, so you see it even if the system is under stress. A click on a pet during that time plays its short greeting, but it can't cut the five minutes short.

## How the timer works

The timer is one small class, `PomodoroTimer` in `src/core/pomodoro.py`. It does exactly one thing, which is a single countdown, and it knows nothing about the pets or the card. The rest of the app just listens to its signals.

**A fixed deadline, not a tick count.** When you start the timer, it records `now + 45 minutes` on a monotonic clock. The remaining time is always the deadline minus the current time. A once-a-second ticker exists only to refresh the display and to notice that the deadline has passed. If the app stalls for a few seconds, the timer doesn't drift or lose time, because nothing is being counted.

**Three signals** carry everything outward:

| Signal | When it fires |
| --- | --- |
| `state_changed(bool)` | The timer started, was cancelled, or finished. The tray and the card use it to flip their buttons. |
| `ticked(int)` | Every second, with the whole seconds remaining. The card uses it for the countdown. |
| `finished()` | The deadline passed. It fires **exactly once per run**, and never when you cancel. |

**A few rules that follow from that:**

- `toggle()` starts the timer if idle and cancels it if running, so one button does both.
- Cancelling doesn't fire `finished()`, which is what keeps a cancelled block from triggering a celebration.
- Starting while a run is active restarts the countdown from the full length.
- It lives on the GUI thread only, and the clock can be swapped for a fake one, which is how the tests drive it without waiting 45 minutes.

When `finished()` fires, the app plays the chime and forces the *pleased* state for five minutes. The lengths are in `src/config.py` (`POMODORO_WORK_MS`, `POMODORO_DONE_MS`). If you want a different length, change them there.

## Why a pet works as a timer

An ordinary timer is a separate thing to start, watch, and be interrupted by. Here it lives in an object that is already part of your desk. Starting it is one click on the card the pets already show. The only thing on the screen during the block is the same cats, and the break signal is a celebration, not an alarm. That gives you a gentler cue to stop, and it reuses an animation that already exists, so the timer cost almost nothing to add. The story of how fast it went in is on [How it works](/internals/how-it-works.qmd).

## Limits

- **The length is fixed at 45 minutes.** There is no setting in the app yet. You change it in `src/config.py`.
- **Quitting the app cancels the timer.** A run isn't saved across restarts. This is deliberate: a block is only a block if you finish it.
- **There is one timer.** There are no breaks, cycles, or counts of completed blocks. Deliberately to keep it simple.
